findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and can be bypassed
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs `where(email: email)` with the raw address, and neither BlockedEmail nor User normalizes case before this check (PostgreSQL string equality is case-sensitive). A blocked address stored as `bad@spamclub.com` will not match a signup attempt with `Bad@SpamClub.com`, so the central block introduced by this PR can be trivially evaded by changing letter case. Blocked emails should be downcased on save and the lookup value downcased (as elsewhere via Email.downcase) before comparison.

findings.title: Validation has a write side-effect that double-counts and races
findings.body: should_block? is called from EmailValidator during ActiveModel validation, yet it increments match_count and saves the record. Validation is not a committed signup attempt and can run multiple times for one attempt — UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save`, which revalidates — so a single blocked signup increments match_count at least twice, and mere `valid?` checks in code/specs also mutate statistics. The read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1; record.save`) is also non-atomic, so concurrent attempts can lose increments. Counting should happen once, atomically (e.g. update_counters/increment_counter), ideally outside pure validation.

findings.title: rejectedEmails array is shared on the controller prototype
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` creates one mutable Ember array on the class prototype shared by all instances of CreateAccountController. `pushObject` in createAccount mutates that shared array rather than per-instance state, so a rejected email leaks into any later/other instance of the signup controller for the lifetime of the page/app and can incorrectly mark that address invalid there. Initialize the array per-instance (e.g. in init) instead of as a prototype property.

findings.title: Domain whitelist/blacklist regexp is not anchored to the end of the address
findings.body: email_in_restriction_setting? builds `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` with no end anchor. For a whitelist entry `good.com`, `attacker@good.com.evil.example` matches and is accepted even though its actual domain is evil.example, defeating the whitelist; conversely blacklist matching can fire on look-alike suffix domains. The pattern should anchor the domain to the end of the address (and properly escape/split the configured domains) rather than matching the whitelisted string anywhere after '@'.
